claim: The COVID-19 pandemic is implicated in the deaths of more than 4 million people worldwide.
source: At the current time, the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic is implicated in the deaths of more than 4 million people worldwide (Dong et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dong et al., 2020

claim: Effective vaccines have been developed to substantially reduce mortality and morbidity due to severe COVID-19.
source: Although effective vaccines have been developed to substantially reduce mortality and morbidity due to severe COVID-19, the emergence of mutated strains of the SARS-CoV-2 virus has challenged the effectiveness of existing vaccines and raised the urgency of identifying alternate therapeutic pathways to target the virus (Tegally, 2020; Erik et al., 2020 ; Collier et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tegally, 2020; Erik et al., 2020; Collier et al., 2021

claim: The emergence of mutated strains of SARS-CoV-2 has challenged the effectiveness of existing vaccines.
source: Although effective vaccines have been developed to substantially reduce mortality and morbidity due to severe COVID-19, the emergence of mutated strains of the SARS-CoV-2 virus has challenged the effectiveness of existing vaccines and raised the urgency of identifying alternate therapeutic pathways to target the virus (Tegally, 2020; Erik et al., 2020 ; Collier et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tegally, 2020; Erik et al., 2020; Collier et al., 2021

claim: Mutated strains of SARS-CoV-2 will likely continue to exploit the same vulnerable host biology to bind onto and infect cells.
source: Nevertheless, it is likely that the mutated strains of SARS-CoV-2 will continue to exploit the same vulnerable host biology to bind onto and infect cells and, in susceptible individuals, evade immune defences and promote the excessive host inflammatory response that is characteristic of severe COVID-19 (Gordon et al., 2020a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gordon et al., 2020a and logical inference

claim: In susceptible individuals, SARS-CoV-2 evades immune defences and promotes excessive host inflammatory response characteristic of severe COVID-19.
source: Nevertheless, it is likely that the mutated strains of SARS-CoV-2 will continue to exploit the same vulnerable host biology to bind onto and infect cells and, in susceptible individuals, evade immune defences and promote the excessive host inflammatory response that is characteristic of severe COVID-19 (Gordon et al., 2020a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gordon et al., 2020a

claim: Host protein mechanisms are independent of genomic mutations in the virus.
source: Therefore, the identification of host proteins that play roles in COVID-19 susceptibility and severity remains crucial to the development of therapeutics as host protein mechanisms are independent of genomic mutations in the virus.
evidence: Based on established biological knowledge

claim: Understanding virus-host pathways may be important in combating viruses beyond SARS-CoV-2.
source: An improved understanding of these therapeutically relevant virus-host pathways may also be important in combating viruses beyond SARS-CoV-2 (Perrin-Cocon et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perrin-Cocon et al., 2020

claim: Large-scale systematic experimental efforts have identified key host proteins that interact with viral proteins in the pathogenesis of severe COVID-19.
source: Several large-scale systematic experimental efforts have identified key host proteins that interact with viral proteins in the pathogenesis of severe COVID-19 (Gordon et al., 2020a; Gordon et al., 2020b; Bouhaddou et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gordon et al., 2020a; Gordon et al., 2020b; Bouhaddou et al., 2020

claim: The spike protein of SARS-CoV-2 mediates virus attachment onto receptors to infect host cells.
source: These notably include efforts to identify direct interactions with the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2, which mediates virus attachment onto receptors to infect host cells and is also the basis of most vaccines (Shang et al., 2020; Harvey et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shang et al., 2020; Harvey et al., 2021

claim: The spike protein of SARS-CoV-2 is the basis of most vaccines.
source: These notably include efforts to identify direct interactions with the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2, which mediates virus attachment onto receptors to infect host cells and is also the basis of most vaccines (Shang et al., 2020; Harvey et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shang et al., 2020; Harvey et al., 2021

claim: Several groups have leveraged genetic datasets of human proteins and COVID-19 disease to identify therapeutically actionable candidate host proteins.
source: To complement in vitro host protein characterisation efforts, several groups have leveraged genetic datasets of human proteins and COVID-19 disease to identify therapeutically actionable candidate host proteins that are likely to play roles in enhancing COVID-19 susceptibility or to be involved in the pathogenesis of severe COVID-19 (Pairo-Castineira et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pairo-Castineira et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021

claim: Mendelian randomisation simulates the design of randomised trials.
source: MR simulates the design of randomised trials, with the underlying principle that randomisation of alleles at conception offers the opportunity to examine approximate differences in average risk of disease between comparable groups in a population that differ only in the distribution of the risk factor of interest (Davies et al., 2018), for example, protein abundance (Zheng et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Davies et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2020

claim: Randomisation of alleles at conception offers the opportunity to examine approximate differences in average risk of disease between comparable groups.
source: MR simulates the design of randomised trials, with the underlying principle that randomisation of alleles at conception offers the opportunity to examine approximate differences in average risk of disease between comparable groups in a population that differ only in the distribution of the risk factor of interest (Davies et al., 2018), for example, protein abundance (Zheng et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Davies et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2020

claim: Clinically actionable proteins identified by the MR approach include IFNAR2, TYK2, OAS1, and IL6R.
source: Some of the clinically actionable proteins identified by the MR approach are part of type I interferon signalling (encoded by genes: IFNAR2, TYK2, OAS1) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) signalling pathways (IL6R).
evidence: Based on inference from the text describing MR approach results

claim: Only OAS1 had evidence of genetic colocalisation among the proteins identified by MR approach.
source: Only one of these proteins (encoded by OAS1) had any evidence of genetic colocalisation, that is, evidence that genetic associations of the protein and COVID outcomes shared the same causal genetic signal (Zhou et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2021

claim: ABO protein was supported by both MR and genetic colocalisation tests.
source: An additional protein that was supported by both MR and genetic colocalisation tests was ABO (Zhou et al., 2021), reported in several published genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of COVID-19 (Pairo-Castineira et al., 2021; Ellinghaus et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2021; Pairo-Castineira et al., 2021; Ellinghaus et al., 2020

claim: The ABO signal is linked with coagulation factors (von Willebrand factor and Factor VIII), IL-6, and CD209/DC-SIGN.
source: In response to the first published GWAS of COVID-19, we reported findings that link the ABO signal with a number of clinically actionable targets including coagulation factors (von Willebrand factor [vWF], and Factor VIII [F8]), IL-6, and CD209/DC-SIGN (Karim et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Karim et al., 2020

claim: Previous MR studies only used curated cis-acting variants as genetic instruments.
source: However, in most of the previous MR studies (Pairo-Castineira et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021), investigators only used curated cis-acting variants (genetic variants near or in the gene encoding the relevant protein) as genetic instruments to represent effects of genetically predicted protein concentrations, rather than genome-wide instruments.
evidence: Supported by citations to Pairo-Castineira et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021

claim: The use of cis-acting variants can minimise the risk of horizontal pleiotropic effects.
source: While the use of cis-acting variants can minimise the risk of horizontal pleiotropic effects (i.e. associations driven by other proteins not on the causal pathway for the disease), it can suffer from lower power than a genome-wide analysis due to fewer available instruments (Zheng et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zheng et al., 2020

claim: The use of cis-acting variants can suffer from lower power than a genome-wide analysis due to fewer available instruments.
source: While the use of cis-acting variants can minimise the risk of horizontal pleiotropic effects (i.e. associations driven by other proteins not on the causal pathway for the disease), it can suffer from lower power than a genome-wide analysis due to fewer available instruments (Zheng et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zheng et al., 2020

claim: Previous protein-COVID-19 MR studies carried out genetic colocalisation tests only for protein-phenotype associations that were significant in the MR analysis.
source: Furthermore, in previous protein-COVID-19 MR studies, genetic colocalisation tests were carried out only for protein-phenotype associations that were significant in the MR analysis, potentially excluding many protein-phenotype associations that may share the same causal genetic signal but are underpowered in a proteome-wide MR approach.
evidence: Based on inference from description of previous studies

claim: The present study undertook a proteome-wide two-sample pan- and cis-MR analysis using the Sun et al. GWAS of plasma protein concentrations and several COVID-19 GWAS phenotypes.
source: In the present study, we expanded on these previous reports by undertaking a proteome-wide two-sample pan- and cis-MR analysis using the Sun et al. GWAS (Sun et al., 2018) of plasma protein concentrations and several COVID-19 GWAS phenotypes from the ICDA COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative (October 2020 release) (Huang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sun et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2020

claim: Genetically predicted circulating ABO protein was associated with COVID-19 susceptibility and severity.
source: First, we showed that genetically predicted circulating ABO protein was associated with COVID-19 susceptibility and severity and the lead ABO signal was associated strongly with plasma concentrations of soluble CD209.
evidence: Based on data from the study's MR analysis

claim: The lead ABO signal was associated strongly with plasma concentrations of soluble CD209.
source: First, we showed that genetically predicted circulating ABO protein was associated with COVID-19 susceptibility and severity and the lead ABO signal was associated strongly with plasma concentrations of soluble CD209.
evidence: Based on data from the study's analysis

claim: CD209 directly interacts with the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2.
source: Second, we collected evidence for a direct mechanism of interaction between the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein and human CD209 protein.
evidence: Based on experimental data from the study

claim: The study performed proteome-wide genetic colocalisation tests followed by single-instrument cis-MR analysis.
source: Third, we performed proteome-wide genetic colocalisation tests, followed by single-instrument cis-MR analysis, and we report additional novel targets of therapeutic relevance.
evidence: Based on the study's methodology

claim: The study used Sun et al. protein GWAS data for the pan-/cis-MR analyses and for performing genetic colocalisation tests.
source: We primarily used Sun et al. protein GWAS data (Sun et al., 2018; Emilsson et al., 2018) for the pan-/cis-MR analyses and for performing genetic colocalisation tests (described below).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sun et al., 2018; Emilsson et al., 2018

claim: Two additional proteomic datasets (Emilsson et al., 2018; Suhre et al., 2017) were used to identify proteins associated with the ABO locus.
source: Two additional proteomic datasets (Emilsson et al., 2018; Suhre et al., 2017) were used to identify proteins associated with the ABO locus.
evidence: Supported by citations to Emilsson et al., 2018; Suhre et al., 2017

claim: All three proteomic studies used the SOMAscan assay platform to detect and quantify protein abundance.
source: All three of the proteomic studies have used the SOMAscan assay platform (an aptamer-based protein detection platform) to detect and quantify protein abundance (Gold et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gold et al., 2012

claim: The study used seven meta-analysed COVID-19 datasets from the October 2020 release of the ICDA COVID-HGI group.
source: We used seven meta-analysed COVID-19 datasets from the October 2020 release of the ICDA COVID-HGI group (https://www.covid19hg.org/results/r4/).
evidence: Based on the study's methodology

claim: Near-independent genetic variants from across the genome were selected as 'pan'-instruments at p≤5 × 10–8.
source: To construct genetic instruments for MR analysis, we selected near-independent (r² = 0.05) genetic variants from across the genome ('pan'-instruments) or from within ±1 Mbp from the transcription start site (TSS) of the gene encoding the protein ('cis'-instruments) associated with the encoded protein abundance at p≤5 × 10–8 for pan-MR analyses and at a less stringent p ≤ 1 × 10⁻⁵ for cis-MR analyses (this p-value corrects for the number of proteins in the druggable genome Schmidt, 2020).
evidence: Based on the study's methodology with citation to Schmidt, 2020

claim: Genetic variants from within ±1 Mbp from the transcription start site of the gene encoding the protein were selected as 'cis'-instruments at p ≤ 1 × 10⁻⁵.
source: To construct genetic instruments for MR analysis, we selected near-independent (r² = 0.05) genetic variants from across the genome ('pan'-instruments) or from within ±1 Mbp from the transcription start site (TSS) of the gene encoding the protein ('cis'-instruments) associated with the encoded protein abundance at p≤5 × 10–8 for pan-MR analyses and at a less stringent p ≤ 1 × 10⁻⁵ for cis-MR analyses (this p-value corrects for the number of proteins in the druggable genome Schmidt, 2020).
evidence: Based on the study's methodology with citation to Schmidt, 2020

claim: The study used the generalised summary data-based Mendelian randomisation (GSMR) approach with the HEIDI-outlier flag turned on.
source: We used the generalised summary data-based Mendelian randomisation (GSMR) approach with the heterogeneity-independent instrument (HEIDI)-outlier flag turned on to carry out the pan- and cis-MR analyses (Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2018

claim: The GSMR software removes potentially pleiotropic instruments and accounts for the residual correlation between instruments.
source: The GSMR software, using the HEIDI-outlier method, removes potentially pleiotropic instruments and accounts for the residual correlation between instruments (important as we are using near-independent genetic instruments).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of the GSMR method

claim: Genotype data from 10,000 randomly sampled UK Biobank participants was used to create a reference LD matrix.
source: To select near-independent genetic instruments and account for linkage disequilibrium (LD) in the MR analyses, we used genotype data from 10,000 randomly sampled UK Biobank participants to create a reference LD matrix, which is ancestry-matched to the pQTL data we used.
evidence: Based on the study's methodology

claim: For each COVID-19 outcome, the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR threshold of 5% was used for significance.
source: For each COVID-19 outcome, we used the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR (False Discovery Rate) threshold of 5% for significance, adjusting for 2042 tests in cis-MR analyses and 1286 tests in pan-MR analyses.
evidence: Based on the study's methodology

claim: The study used the Bayesian method of genetic colocalisation implemented in the coloc R package.
source: To identify shared causal genetic signals between protein and COVID outcomes, we used the Bayesian method of genetic colocalisation implemented in the coloc R package (Giambartolomei, 2014) using the marginal association statistics for each trait (i.e. assuming one independent signal in each region).
evidence: Supported by citation to Giambartolomei, 2014

claim: A posterior probability for shared causal genetic signal (PP.H4) threshold of more than 0.8 was used to identify shared causal genetic variants.
source: For each COVID-19 outcome, a posterior probability for shared causal genetic signal (PP.H4) threshold of more than 0.8 was used to identify shared causal genetic variants.
evidence: Based on the study's methodology

claim: Recombinant human receptors and SARS-CoV-2 spike protein extracellular domains were expressed and purified as previously described.
source: Recombinant human receptors and SARS-CoV-2 spike protein extracellular domains were expressed and purified as previously described (Shilts et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shilts et al., 2021

claim: The pan-MR analysis revealed nine distinct protein probes associated with four COVID outcomes at an FDR of 5%.
source: Overall, the pan-MR analysis revealed nine distinct protein probes associated with four COVID outcomes at an FDR of 5% (Figure 1A).
evidence: Based on data from the study's pan-MR analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: The pQTLs selected by GSMR to represent nine probes were also cis-eQTLs.
source: The pQTLs selected by GSMR to represent these nine probes were also cis-eQTLs (as curated for the Open Targets Genetics portal Open Targets Genetics, 2019) and, except the ABO signal via rs8176719-insertionC (will be referred to as rs8176719-insC – a frameshift mutation that inserts a guanine nucleotide in the 258th position of exon 6), were not missense variants or in LD with missense variants (Supplementary file 3), minimising the possibility that SNPs with artefactual associations with proteins were used as genetic instruments for the majority of significant pan-MR association.
evidence: Based on data from the study's analysis with citation to Open Targets Genetics, 2019

claim: Three proteins with pan-MR associations were supported by corresponding cis-MR associations: ABO, ICAM-1, and IL-6R.
source: Three proteins with pan-MR associations were supported by corresponding cis-MR associations (Figure 1A and B, Supplementary file 4): ABO, ICAM-1, and IL-6R.
evidence: Based on data from the study's MR analysis shown in Figure 1A and B

claim: Only ABO and IL-6R proteins had evidence of genetic colocalisation with posterior probabilities more than 0.9 and 0.4, respectively.
source: Among these three, only ABO and IL-6R proteins had some evidence of genetic colocalisation with posterior probabilities (PP.H4) more than 0.9 and 0.4, respectively, of a shared genetic signal between protein and COVID-19 phenotype (Figure 2).
evidence: Based on data from the study's colocalisation analysis shown in Figure 2

claim: Genetically predicted ABO concentration was associated with risk in four out of seven COVID-19 outcomes.
source: Genetically predicted ABO concentration was associated with risk in four out of seven COVID-19 outcomes (Figure 2).
evidence: Based on data from the study's MR analysis shown in Figure 2

claim: Genetically predicted ABO concentration was associated with COVID-19 vs. population with cis-MR odds ratio of 1.08 [1.05, 1.10], p=7 × 10–10.
source: These four outcomes represented both susceptibility (e.g. COVID-19 vs. population, cis-MR odds ratio [OR] [95% CI] per SD genetically predicted ABO concentrations: 1.08 [1.05, 1.10], p=7 × 10–10) and severity (e.g. hospitalised COVID-19 vs. population, cis-MR OR [95% CI]: 1.12 [1.08, 1.17], p=1 × 10–8) of COVID-19.
evidence: Based on data from the study's cis-MR analysis

claim: Genetically predicted ABO concentration was associated with hospitalised COVID-19 vs. population with cis-MR odds ratio of 1.12 [1.08, 1.17], p=1 × 10–8.
source: These four outcomes represented both susceptibility (e.g. COVID-19 vs. population, cis-MR odds ratio [OR] [95% CI] per SD genetically predicted ABO concentrations: 1.08 [1.05, 1.10], p=7 × 10–10) and severity (e.g. hospitalised COVID-19 vs. population, cis-MR OR [95% CI]: 1.12 [1.08, 1.17], p=1 × 10–8) of COVID-19.
evidence: Based on data from the study's cis-MR analysis

claim: Genetically predicted soluble IL-6R was associated with higher risk of hospitalised COVID-19 compared to population-based controls with cis-MR OR of 0.94 [0.91, 0.97], p=8 × 10–4.
source: Genetically predicted soluble IL-6R was only associated with higher risk of hospitalised COVID-19 compared to population-based controls (cis-MR OR [95% CI] per SD genetically predicted IL-6R: 0.94 [0.91, 0.97], p=8 × 10–4) (Figure 2).
evidence: Based on data from the study's cis-MR analysis shown in Figure 2

claim: All probes except IL-6R and ABO had at least one trans-acting SNP, and in all these cases, at least one of the trans-acting SNPs were assigned to the ABO gene.
source: When examining the SNPs involved in the pan-MR associations of the nine probes, all probes except IL-6R and ABO had at least one trans-acting SNP, and in all these cases, at least one of the trans-acting SNPs were assigned to the ABO gene by the Open Targets Genetics V2G pipeline (Table 1), re-confirming the pervasive pleiotropy of the ABO genetic signal.
evidence: Based on data from the study's analysis shown in Table 1

claim: The ABO signal rs8176719-insC showed the strongest association with higher plasma concentrations of soluble CD209 in all three datasets.
source: Aside from the ABO protein, the ABO signal rs8176719-insC showed the strongest association (Sun et al: p=6.03 × 10–258, Emilsson et al: p=1.00 × 10–307, Suhre et al: p=1.27 × 10–75) with higher plasma concentrations of soluble CD209 in all three datasets (associations from two datasets illustrated in Figure 3, and associations from all three datasets tabulated in Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Based on data from the study's analysis shown in Figure 3 and Supplementary file 6

claim: Purified spike protein could directly attach onto human cells expressing CD209 but not control cells.
source: We found that purified spike protein indeed could directly attach onto human cells expressing CD209 but not control cells, suggesting that CD209 could act as a receptor for viral attachment onto host cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: Based on experimental data from the study shown in Figure 4A

claim: CD209 could act as a receptor for viral attachment onto host cells.
source: We found that purified spike protein indeed could directly attach onto human cells expressing CD209 but not control cells, suggesting that CD209 could act as a receptor for viral attachment onto host cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: In a direct binding assay, binding between soluble CD209 and the viral spike protein was specific and comparable to ACE2.
source: Furthermore in a direct binding assay testing purified soluble CD209 and the viral spike protein, we could detect binding that was specific and comparable to the primary known receptor for SARS-CoV-2, ACE2 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Based on experimental data from the study shown in Figure 4B

claim: The coloc-first approach identified four proteins (ABO, FAS, OAS1, THBS3) with evidence of genetic colocalisation (PP.H4 >0.8) with four out of seven COVID-19 phenotypes.
source: This 'coloc-first' approach identified four proteins (ABO, FAS, OAS1, THBS3) with evidence of genetic colocalisation (PP.H4 >0.8) with four out of seven COVID-19 phenotypes (Figure 5).
evidence: Based on data from the study's colocalisation analysis shown in Figure 5

claim: FAS and THBS3 are not reported in proteomic MR studies of COVID-19 to date.
source: Two of these (FAS and THBS3) are, to the best of our knowledge, not reported in proteomic MR studies of COVID-19 to date which have only examined for colocalisation evidence after MR.
evidence: Based on inference from literature review

claim: There was evidence of genetic colocalisation between the ABO protein and six out of seven COVID-19 phenotypes.
source: Consistent with pan- and cis-MR findings, there was evidence of genetic colocalisation between the ABO protein and six out of seven COVID-19 phenotypes (Figure 6), with similar MR estimates when the colocalising SNP was used to perform single-SNP cis-MR.
evidence: Based on data from the study's colocalisation analysis shown in Figure 6

claim: The coloc-first approach revealed a common genetic signal between OAS1 and COVID-19 in two out of seven COVID-19 phenotypes (PP.H4 = 0.88 in COVID-19 vs. population, and 0.82 in hospitalised COVID-19 vs. population).
source: The coloc-first approach revealed a common genetic signal between OAS1 and COVID-19 in two out of seven COVID-19 phenotypes (PP.H4 = 0.88 in COVID-19 vs. population, and 0.82 in hospitalised COVID-19 vs. population).
evidence: Based on data from the study's colocalisation analysis

claim: The SNPs representing the common genetic signal between OAS1 and COVID-19 phenotypes were missense variants in OAS1 gene or in LD with missense variants at r2 >0.8.
source: However, the SNPs representing the common genetic signal between OAS1 and COVID-19 phenotypes (12:112919637:G:A and 12:112919388:G:A) were missense variants in OAS1 gene or in LD with missense variants at r2 >0.8, rendering their effect estimates potentially biased due to aptamer binding effects (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Based on data from the study's analysis

claim: The same variants have effects on gene expression, which is independent of aptamer binding.
source: Despite this, the same variants have effects on gene expression (as assessed in any of several tissues curated by Open Targets Genetics Open Targets Genetics, 2019), which is independent of aptamer binding, suggesting that causal inference regarding OAS1 protein and COVID-19 risk may still be valid.
evidence: Based on data from Open Targets Genetics with citation to Open Targets Genetics, 2019

claim: Genetically predicted higher OAS1 was associated with lower risk of severe COVID-19 vs. population (OR 0.52 [0.42, 0.65], p=5 × 10–9).
source: In single-SNP MR analyses, genetically predicted higher OAS1 was associated with lower risk of severe COVID-19 vs. population (OR [95% CI] per SD genetically predicted OAS1 concentrations: 0.52 [0.42, 0.65], p=5 × 10–9), hospitalised COVID-19 vs. population (0.63 [0.53, 0.75], p=1 × 10–7) and susceptibility to COVID-19 vs. population (0.79 [0.71, 0.87], p=2 × 10–6).
evidence: Based on data from the study's single-SNP MR analysis

claim: Genetically predicted higher OAS1 was associated with lower risk of hospitalised COVID-19 vs. population (OR 0.63 [0.53, 0.75], p=1 × 10–7).
source: In single-SNP MR analyses, genetically predicted higher OAS1 was associated with lower risk of severe COVID-19 vs. population (OR [95% CI] per SD genetically predicted OAS1 concentrations: 0.52 [0.42, 0.65], p=5 × 10–9), hospitalised COVID-19 vs. population (0.63 [0.53, 0.75], p=1 × 10–7) and susceptibility to COVID-19 vs. population (0.79 [0.71, 0.87], p=2 × 10–6).
evidence: Based on data from the study's single-SNP MR analysis

claim: Genetically predicted higher OAS1 was associated with lower susceptibility to COVID-19 vs. population (OR 0.79 [0.71, 0.87], p=2 × 10–6).
source: In single-SNP MR analyses, genetically predicted higher OAS1 was associated with lower risk of severe COVID-19 vs. population (OR [95% CI] per SD genetically predicted OAS1 concentrations: 0.52 [0.42, 0.65], p=5 × 10–9), hospitalised COVID-19 vs. population (0.63 [0.53, 0.75], p=1 × 10–7) and susceptibility to COVID-19 vs. population (0.79 [0.71, 0.87], p=2 × 10–6).
evidence: Based on data from the study's single-SNP MR analysis

claim: Genetically predicted elevated FAS was associated with a higher risk of severe COVID-19 (OR 1.38 [1.17, 1.62], p=1 × 10–4).
source: Genetically predicted elevated FAS (indicated by two FAS probes: FAS.9459.7.3 and FAS.5392.73.2) and THBS3 were associated with a higher risk of severe COVID-19 (OR [95% CI] per SD genetically predicted FAS concentrations indicated by FAS.9459.7.3: 1.38 [1.17, 1.62], p=1 × 10–4) and COVID-19 vs. lab/self-reported negative COVID-19 (OR [95% CI] per SD genetically predicted THBS3 concentrations: 1.70 [1.30, 2.22], p=9 × 10–5), respectively.
evidence: Based on data from the study's single-SNP MR analysis

claim: Genetically predicted elevated THBS3 was associated with COVID-19 vs. lab/self-reported negative COVID-19 (OR 1.70 [1.30, 2.22], p=9 × 10–5).
source: Genetically predicted elevated FAS (indicated by two FAS probes: FAS.9459.7.3 and FAS.5392.73.2) and THBS3 were associated with a higher risk of severe COVID-19 (OR [95% CI] per SD genetically predicted FAS concentrations indicated by FAS.9459.7.3: 1.38 [1.17, 1.62], p=1 × 10–4) and COVID-19 vs. lab/self-reported negative COVID-19 (OR [95% CI] per SD genetically predicted THBS3 concentrations: 1.70 [1.30, 2.22], p=9 × 10–5), respectively.
evidence: Based on data from the study's single-SNP MR analysis

claim: The ABO signal was associated with monocyte count, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), and pulmonary embolism (PE).
source: For example, the ABO signal was associated with monocyte count, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), and pulmonary embolism (PE).
evidence: Based on data from the study's PheWAS analysis

claim: OAS1 and THBS3 variants were associated with platelet counts.
source: OAS1 and THBS3 variants were associated with platelet counts.
evidence: Based on data from the study's PheWAS analysis

claim: The soluble Fas receptor is reported to act as a decoy receptor competing with the trans-membrane Fas receptor for Fas ligand.
source: The soluble Fas receptor is reported to act as a decoy receptor competing with the trans-membrane Fas receptor for Fas ligand (FasL) (Cheng, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cheng, 1994

claim: Genetically predicted higher circulating sFas is likely to represent effects of lower Fas-FasL signalling.
source: Genetically predicted higher circulating sFas is, therefore, likely to represent effects of lower Fas-FasL signalling and, in our study, was associated with a higher risk of very severe COVID-19.
evidence: Based on inference from biological knowledge and study data

claim: Fas-FasL signalling typically initiates a cascade of intracellular programmes that result in cell death or apoptosis.
source: Fas-FasL signalling typically initiates a cascade of intracellular programmes that result in cell death or apoptosis.
evidence: Based on established biological knowledge

claim: Fas-mediated apoptosis plays a central role in T- and B-cell homeostasis.
source: Fas-mediated apoptosis plays a central role in T- and B-cell homeostasis (Hao, 2008), preventing the emergence of autoreactive or overactive immune cells (Hao, 2008; Butt, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hao, 2008; Butt, 2015

claim: Excessive inflammation by hyperactive T-cells and autoantibodies was reported to underlie several cases of severe COVID-19.
source: Excessive inflammation by hyperactive T-cells and autoantibodies was reported to underlie several cases of severe COVID-19 (Khamsi, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Khamsi, 2021

claim: Fas-mediated apoptosis of virus-infected cells is a major mechanism of resolution of viral infections.
source: Furthermore, Fas-mediated apoptosis of virus-infected cells is a major mechanism of resolution of viral infections (Thomson, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thomson, 2001

claim: Delayed apoptosis is reported to be one of the strategies exploited by SARS-CoV-2 in the early stages of infection to facilitate viral replication.
source: Delayed apoptosis is reported to be one of the strategies exploited by SARS-CoV-2 in the early stages of infection to facilitate viral replication (Thomson, 2001; Ivanisenko et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Thomson, 2001; Ivanisenko et al., 2020

claim: Fas is one of the major targets of lopinavir-ritonavir.
source: For example, Fas is one of the major targets of lopinavir-ritonavir – a combination HIV protease inhibitor (Sorbera et al., 2020); clinical trials of lopinavir-ritonavir failed to provide any therapeutic benefits beyond standard care in hospitalised COVID-19 patients (Cao et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sorbera et al., 2020
